hotspots.name: Islais Creek estuary
hotspots.description: Fresh water from uphill springs flowed into saltwater marshlands on the bay's east shore, before the shoreline and creek were filled in and the creek channelized.

sources.title: Islais Creek (Port of San Francisco)

hotspots.name: Laguna Honda
hotspots.description: A natural lake before it was dammed and enlarged for the city's water supply; a second natural lake, near Seventh Avenue and Lawton, was filled in early last century.

sources.title: Laguna Honda (FoundSF, quoting Gilliam, The Natural World of San Francisco)

hotspots.name: Lake Merced
hotspots.description: A freshwater lake that was once a lagoon fed by streams, groundwater and an ocean channel; drifting dunes cut that link, though storms and quakes reopened it, and a tail ran to Ocean Beach as late as the 1800s.

sources.title: San Francisco's Lake Merced: Native Wetland (Western Neighborhoods Project)
Lake Merced (Wikipedia)

hotspots.name: Lobos Creek
hotspots.description: One of the few small flowing creeks of the old peninsula, its banks lined with riparian woodland and scrub of coast live oak, willow and Pacific wax myrtle.

sources.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: the unique natural landscape of San Francisco (SFEI Hidden Nature SF story map)

hotspots.name: Mission Bay and Mission Creek marsh
hotspots.description: An estuary of freshwater marsh, saltwater marsh, tidal mudflats and shallow bay, fed by Mission Creek, whose mouth lay near today's Berry Street between 7th and 8th.

sources.title: Natural History of Mission Bay, Chris Carlsson (FoundSF)

hotspots.name: Mountain Lake
hotspots.description: A dune-dammed headwater lake: drainage pooled behind sand mounds. Dune-dammed lakes like this provided habitat for species such as California red-legged frogs and San Francisco garter snakes.

sources.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: the unique natural landscape of San Francisco (SFEI Hidden Nature SF story map)

hotspots.name: Precita Creek
hotspots.description: A small stream running from near Market and 24th Streets along today's Precita Avenue and Cesar Chavez Street into Islais Creek's estuarine bog.

sources.title: Precita Creek (Wikipedia)

hotspots.name: South of Market fens
hotspots.description: Rare peat-soil fens, likely relics of the last ice age, lay in low ground between dune ridges and along tidal marsh edges in today's SoMa; in 1896 a botanist described one as an 'Arctic oasis' amid California vegetation.

sources.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: the unique natural landscape of San Francisco (SFEI Hidden Nature SF story map)

hotspots.name: Washerwoman's Lagoon
hotspots.description: A freshwater lagoon held back by dunes and beaches, in what is now the Marina District, beyond Russian Hill and toward the Presidio.

sources.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: the unique natural landscape of San Francisco (SFEI Hidden Nature SF story map)
Washerwoman's Lagoon (FoundSF)

hotspots.name: Western mobile dune sheet
hotspots.description: A vast sheet of loose, shifting sand on the peninsula's west side, sparsely vegetated; Coast Survey maps show its edge moved up to a quarter mile in about twenty years.

sources.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: the unique natural landscape of San Francisco (SFEI Hidden Nature SF story map)

hotspots.name: Yerba Buena Cove
hotspots.description: A cove on the bay shore between Clarks Point and Rincon Point; its beach lay as far back as today's Montgomery Street until Gold Rush filling put downtown over it.

sources.title: Yerba Buena Cove (Wikipedia)

villages.name: Amuctac
villages.description: General location of a Yelamu village site around Visitacion Valley, around the time of Spanish contact. Approximate: villages were places and the people who lived there, and they moved seasonally and over time. Source: SFEI Hidden Nature SF, after Milliken (1983, 1995) and the National Park Service (2009).
